title: Vendor operational limits mapping for platforms
content:
Purpose
This note maps practical, operational limits customers encounter on hyperscaler managed AI endpoints (AWS/GCP/Azure) and shows how to position Redwood with concrete win themes and tactical rebuttals. Target audience: platform/SRE buyers, infra architects, and technical sellers prepping demos or RFP responses.

Executive summary (one sentence)
Hyperscaler managed endpoints trade simplicity for opaque operational limits: unpredictable throttling, coarse telemetry, limited failover controls, and constrained migration paths — all of which create day-one risk for platform teams. Redwood’s messaging should focus on deterministic controls, transparent economics, and migration-safe fallbacks.

Observed operational limits and buyer pain (field notes)
- Concurrency and throttling: vendor quotas are often undocumented per-instance concurrency ceilings; when workload patterns shift, customers hit soft limits causing large tail latencies.
- Cold starts and warm pool controls: limited visibility into warm pool size and lifecycle, leading to burst latency spikes. Customers can’t reliably size transient workloads.
- Capacity elasticity and cost shocks: automatic scaling heuristics sometimes scale inefficiently (over-provision then throttle) resulting in surprise bills. Billing granularity rarely aligns with token-level economics.
- Multi-tenant isolation guarantees: shared pools can surface noisy neighbor effects; enterprise buyers flag this as an unacceptable risk for latency-sensitive features.
- Telemetry and observability granularity: telemetry often surfaces only aggregate metrics (calls/sec, avg latency) without token-level latency distributions, KV cache hit rates, or per-model tail analysis — blockers for SLA verification.
- Model version and rollout control: limited ability to pin versions across instances or orchestrate canary rollouts with deterministic traffic splits and instant rollback.
- Network and data egress constraints: managed endpoints introduce extra network tiers and unpredictable egress paths; regulatory buyers worry about data residency and auditability.
- Hidden compatibility gaps: vendor-managed stacks may not support certain quantized kernels or custom compilation paths customers rely on for cost/latency profiles.

Implications for buyers
- Platform teams adopt complex wrappers or replicate workloads off-vendor to regain control, increasing ops burden.
- Product teams see inconsistent user experience during traffic spikes, which impacts core metrics (engagement/retention).
- Cost forecasting becomes a major procurement friction item — finance teams demand predictable unit economics.

Redwood positioning angles and concrete win themes
- Deterministic SLO controls: emphasize per-route latency SLOs, predictable batching, and capacity reservations. Demo scenario: show identical workload on vendor endpoint vs Redwood Dedicated with steady p95 under high-concurrency.
- Transparent unit economics: provide token-level cost reports and per-token latency cost breakdowns. Win theme: "what you pay for is what you can measure."
- Configurable warm pools & graceful warm/cold behavior: show warm pool sizing and burst policies customers can tune. Buyer impact: reduced tail latency and predictable UX during launches.
- Rollouts & model pinning primitives: highlight canary/A-B with instant fallback and model-variant routing based on real-time error/quality signals.
- Migration safety and escape hatch: concrete migration playbook (prefix cache warm-up, dual-writing inference, staged DNS cutovers). Win theme: "lift-and-shift without dropping quality or SLOs."
- Telemetry depth: token-level histograms, KV cache hit/miss, per-model token throughput, and automated anomaly alerts tied to eval sets.
- Isolation options: dedicated pools or VPC/private deployments for regulated customers. Frame as: "same API, stronger guarantees."

Tactical rebuttals and messaging snippets (for sellers)
- Objection: "Hyperscalers give us easy ops and fast time-to-market." Rebuttal: "Initial speed hides operational debt — we offer fast onboarding plus controls that avoid rework when you scale to 10x traffic."
- Objection: "Pricing is lower on vendor endpoints for low volume." Rebuttal: "True at tiny scale; we beat total cost at production due to batching, quantization, and predictable reserved capacity. We’ll run a short PoC to quantify that for you."
- Objection: "We rely on managed endpoints to avoid infra headaches." Rebuttal: "Our Private and Dedicated options remove infra headaches while keeping the same developer API — plus SRE-grade tools for your team to operate with confidence."

Demo checklist (ops-focused)
- Load-profile: ramp to 2–3x expected concurrency and show p50/p95/p99 comparison.
- Failure injection: simulate a regional outage and demonstrate Redwood routing/fallback to pinned variants.
- Billing transparency: show token-level billing dashboard and explain anomaly detection.
- Rollout test: deploy model canary, run A/B for 30 minutes, then instant rollback and show no client-visible errors.

Suggested battle-card fields (one-liners sellers can memorize)
- Hyperscaler: "Easy start, muddy guarantees."
- Redwood: "Predictable serving — measurable cost and SLOs you can test."
- When to choose them: hyperscaler for prototyping and non-SLA workloads; Redwood for production, regulated, or latency-critical features.
- Quick win play: reserved capacity + warm-pool tuning that removes 95th-99th percentile tail from customer-critical paths.

Objections we should pre-empt in collateral
- "We don’t want vendor lock-in": publish a migration checklist + compatibility matrix (models, quant levels, compilation paths).
- "We need single-pane console for billing": emphasize console integrations and exported BI artifacts plus scheduled reports that mirror finance flows.
- "Managed endpoints already integrate with our cloud IAM": call out our KMS/HSM and SSO integrations for Private deployments to match enterprise security needs.

Open questions to validate with product/eng (for future collateral)
- Exact warm-pool lifecycle metric names and UI copy to demonstrate in demos.
- Quantization compatibility matrix we can hand to prospects (per-model, per-arch).
- Short PoC template for cost parity experiments (sample dataset, ramp plan, acceptance criteria).

Next steps for GTM
- Build a 1-pager "Ops risk checklist" that sellers can attach to invites (three pages: quick checklist, demo plan, migration summary).
- Create a short runbook for PoC (2-week guide) that includes billing instrumentation, traffic shaping, and success criteria.
- Ship a lightweight battle-card (single sheet) and rehearse with SRE-focused AE motion.

Notes to self / informal fragments
- Add field notes from two recent calls (Company X latency incident, Company Y finance gating on invoices).
- Explore partnership language for MSPs who handle on-prem migrations.

End of note.
